questions.stem: A 5 kg object is lifted to a height of 3 m. Using g = 10 m/s^2, what is the gravitational potential energy gained?
questions.explanation: GPE = m x g x h = 5 x 10 x 3 = 150 J. Option A (15 J) results from forgetting g. Option C (50 J) results from using only m x g without height. Option D incorrectly multiplies by an extra factor.

questions.stem: A roller coaster car at the top of a 40 m hill has 200 000 J of gravitational potential energy. Using g = 10 m/s^2, what is the mass of the car?
questions.explanation: Rearranging GPE = mgh gives m = GPE / (g x h) = 200 000 / (10 x 40) = 200 000 / 400 = 500 kg. Option A (5000 kg) results from dividing by height only. Option B (800 kg) comes from an incorrect calculation. Option C forgets to account for gravity.

questions.stem: A window cleaner carries a 2 kg bucket up a 10 m ladder, then down to a platform 6 m above the ground. What is the net change in GPE of the bucket from the ground? (g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: The net height change is from ground (0 m) to the platform (6 m), so the height gained is 6 m. GPE = mgh = 2 x 10 x 6 = 120 J. It does not matter that the bucket went to 10 m first; the GPE depends only on the final height relative to the starting point. Option A uses 10 m. Option D adds both heights.

questions.stem: A 60 kg person climbs stairs and gains 1800 J of gravitational potential energy. How high did they climb? (g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: h = GPE / (m x g) = 1800 / (60 x 10) = 1800 / 600 = 3 m. Option A (30 m) results from dividing by mass only. Option B (0.3 m) results from dividing by mass x g x an extra factor. Option D (18 m) results from dividing by g only.

questions.stem: A hydroelectric power station uses water falling from a reservoir 80 m above the turbines. If 500 kg of water falls, how much gravitational potential energy is converted? (g = 10 m/s^2)
questions.explanation: GPE = mgh = 500 x 10 x 80 = 400 000 J (400 kJ). This is a real-world application: hydroelectric power stations convert the GPE of stored water into kinetic energy of falling water, then into electrical energy via turbines and generators. Option A forgets one factor, and Option D multiplies by an extra 10.
